query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an optimized amount of graphene nanoplatelets into a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will induce the formation of a durable, lubricious tribofilm during sliding, resulting in consistently lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates from room temperature to 800 °C under variable load and environmental conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Pure CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with homogeneous microstructure and standard tribological behavior across the temperature range.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of an optimized, low weight fraction of graphene nanoplatelets into the alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under variable loads and typical dry or controlled environmental exposures.
generation.structural_mediator: A well-dispersed graphene network that forms an in-situ tribofilm at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: The graphene nanoplatelets act as solid lubricants by aligning under stress to form a continuous, low-shear-strength tribofilm, which not only reduces direct metal-to-metal contact but also mitigates oxidation and plastic deformation, thereby lowering friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The graphene-doped CoCrFeNi alloy will exhibit significantly lower steady-state friction coefficients and wear rates compared to the unmodified alloy over the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The standard CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without graphene addition, which struggles to maintain low friction and wear rates across the wide temperature range.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under sliding conditions up to 800 °C and under load conditions typical of high-performance tribological applications; extreme loads, environments that aggressively oxidize or chemically attack graphene, or temperatures beyond 800 °C may fall outside these boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum weight fraction and dispersion uniformity of graphene nanoplatelets needed for maximum tribofilm stability remain to be determined, and the effectiveness under different environmental atmospheres (e.g., inert vs. oxidative) may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the pure CoCrFeNi alloy (baseline) and one doped with an optimized content of graphene nanoplatelets. Conduct standardized ball-on-disk sliding tribometry tests across a temperature gradient from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled loads and identical environmental conditions. After testing, use scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to analyze the formation and integrity of the tribofilm on the wear tracks.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (steady-state value at each temperature)
Wear rate (volumetric wear loss per unit load and distance)
Tribofilm thickness and continuity (via SEM/EDS analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the graphene-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across the entire temperature range (RT to 800 °C) compared to the pure alloy, or if no consistent tribofilm formation is observed under the tested conditions.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, WC-FeCoCrNi composites were prepared by the SPS process. The effects of WC content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and wear resistance of WC–HEA composites were studied. The main conclusions are as follows: A single-phase FCC solid solution structure was formed after SPS sintering of the HEA pure matrix powder, which did not appear before sintering, indicating that SPS is helpful for HEA to complete alloying. The sintered WC–HEA composite is mainly composed of an FCC matrix phase (Ni, Fe) and carbide phases (Cr7C3, Co3W3C, WC, etc.). With the increase of WC content, the distribution of WC is dispersed, and the content of Cr7C3 and Co3W3C increases gradually. Some needle-like Cr-rich phases in the FCC matrix coarsen into flakes. Although the addition of WC reduces the densification of the composite to a certain extent, it significantly improves the hardness and compressive yield strength of the matrix. The microhardness of the 30 WC–HEA composite is the highest, at 459.2 HV, which is 71.2% higher than that of the pure matrix material. High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature.
